newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Maskhadov says Chechnya may turn to Middle East.
newsitem.headline: Maskhadov says Chechnya may turn to Middle East.

text.p: Chechnya's President Aslan Maskhadov said his mainly Moslem separatist republic might have to turn towards the Middle East if Moscow continued what he called its "economic blockade", Interfax news agency said.

In a message addressed to Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Maskhadov said: "If these attempts (to isolate Chechnya) continue, we shall be compelled to seek trade partners among the countries of the Middle East."

The message, handed to Russian officials by Maskhadov's aide Ruslan Kutayev, came as talks on funding between Moscow and its rebellious Caucasian territory remained stalled over Chechnya's final political status.

Moscow and Chechnya signed a ceasefire last August, halting a 21-month war. Under the peace deal a final decision on Chechnya's status would be deferred for five years but Maskhadov regards his region as de facto independent.
Individual fighters from the Middle East helped Chechen separatists during their conflict with Moscow and Maskhadov travelled to Saudi Arabia last week for the traditional Moslem pilgrimage or haj.
But no other country has recognised Chechnya as a separate state and it needs Russian help to rebuild its war-shattered economy and infrastructure.
In his message Maskhadov also urged Chernomyrdin to hand over Chechens from the former pro-Moscow administration in Grozny who he said had stolen large sums of money.
On Tuesday the outgoing head of the OSCE's mission to Chechnya, Tim Guldimann, expressed hope that a lasting peace settlement was possible but warned against complacency.

"The war is over but there is a danger that the whole process (of normalising ties) may not go as well or as swiftly as it should for the resolution of problems that still exist," the Swiss diplomat told Ekho Moskvy radio.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) supervised the elections in January that swept Maskhadov, a former guerrilla commander, to power.
Underlining the sense of uncertainty still persisting in Chechnya, an explosive device went off in central Grozny on Tuesday, though nobody was hurt, Interfax reported.
It said the blast occurred at a crossroads as a senior security official passed by in a car. Interfax gave no further details on the incident.

On Monday a bomb damaged a monument to union between Russia and the autonomous region of Kabardino-Balkaria in the city of Nalchik some 70 km (45 miles) from Chechnya's borders, raising the spectre that separatists could be taking the independence struggle outside their tiny, mountainous territory.
Nobody claimed responsibility for the incident.
